And Egyptians were known for burying the first emperor of China with terracotta warriors and wealth, which doesn't make sense. If you die, you die. So why is this happening? Money, capital, too much of it changes the fundamental chemistry of the brain. It makes you crazy. Let's do a thought experiment. Satan comes into this room and says, "I'll give you a billion dollars but you have to live forever and be my slave." We'd say no. But if we are the richest people on earth with $10 billion now, and he says, "You can keep your money but you must live forever and be my slave," we would agree. That's the difference money makes.

Bronze started as a weapon for power but became jewelry and pottery to show status over time because rich people wanted it. As everyone wanted bronze, it became currency stored easily, universally recognized, and mobile over centuries. This is how capital forms—universal, valuable, permanent, and mobile. 

Capital needs universality; the more people want it, the more valuable it is. It must store value, be permanent, mobile, and rare enough to become a currency. Throughout history, we've used different sources like sea shells, cattle, grain, women, slaves, drugs, oil, bronze, gold, and US dollars. Money has always signified unpayable debt. David Grabbe, an anthropologist, wrote in his book *Debt* that money arises from transactions where debt can't be paid off.

The first example is killing a brother; you acknowledge the debt by giving something valuable. Second, if a woman marries into your family, you give her a gift to balance the loss of a daughter. The third and most important example is honoring great people in your community by burying them with gifts, acknowledging their contributions. This is why we find graves laden with gold from ancient times.
